chapter: Recent years and early piano influences
title: Alex Hill as arranger and composer
summary: Ramirez praises Alex Hill's intuition for vocals and orchestration and his trouble finding Hill's music.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: There was also another one there, Alex Hill.
Well, didn't he come from Chicago?
I don't know where he came from.

But he was a very... He was, I don't know, like... He had the...what do I want to say...? He had the instinct. He had the instinct of creativeness for vocalists; I mean, for vocal backing, you know -- and for the voice and singing and for the lyric. He was descriptive also, and he had a thing... His intuition as far as the
orchestra was concerned was a little sharper and, you know, the pianistic approach.

Now, to me, I think... It's pretty difficult for a pianist, I find, to sit down and to arrange, you know, or compose, because he is always creating in his mind. That's the way I figure. Before you put it on paper, you have three or four variations already going on, you know. As a pure discipline, by a one-note instrument, you are able to put down much more...you know, able to write parts. But he had the intuition of an orchestrator.
He did quite a bit of that, I think, didn't he?

Yeah. I just saw one or two compositions, and I was rehearsing a singer...you know, he was coaching a singer to sing one of his songs -- which I don't remember exactly what it was. But I was impressed by the way he... by his work, you know.
He made a few records with a band, and then... He went to work for Irving Mills for a time, I think.
Oh! I've been trying to find some of his music; it's very difficult.
